https://www.thetimes.com/uk/science/arti.title: Walden review — Gemma Arterton gets a bit lost in woods of eco-drama
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/science/arti.subtitle: Harold Pinter Theatre, SW1
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/science/arti.text:
★★★☆☆You certainly can’t accuse the producer Sonia Friedman of going for the easy option of reopening in the West End with a tried and tested favourite. Instead, her Re:Emerge season greets the new, post-vaccine dawn with a debut play by a young American writer in which mankind is making plans to escape the scourge of global warming by colonising Mars.
Big ideas indeed. And along with a meditation on our place in the galaxy, there is a sprinkling of stardust in the form of Gemma Arterton. It’s not quite enough, though.
Amy Berryman’s ecological drama — tastefully directed by Ian Rickson — struggles to get its heavy payload off the ground. The characters are symbols rather than flesh-and-blood humans, their high-minded conversations taking their cue — as the title suggests — from Henry David Thoreau’s classic reflections on the joys of a simple life in the woods. On her Twitter profile, Berryman describes herself not just as a writer but as a “climate advocate”. Walden is an apocalyptic vision that sometimes comes close to turning into a well-intentioned lecture.
Rae Smith’s pastoral cabin set is immaculately lit by Azusa Ono.
We are visiting the “not-so-distant future”, as the play text puts it.
Berryman introduces us to Stella, a former Nasa architect who has dropped out and embarked on a new, technology-lite existence far from the teeming, overheated cities. She shares a home there with Bryan, a gentle, home brew-loving member of Earth Advocates, a mass movement that could well be the descendant of today’s Extinction Rebellion.
The news is full of reports of a mega tsunami in Asia; the world is falling apart.
Amid this turmoil, Stella tries to salvage her relationship with her estranged twin sister, Cassie, a Nasa botanist who has returned from a year-long stint on the moon, and who is in line to lead the all-important mission to Mars. The women happen to be the daughters of a famous astronaut. But if Stella has already renounced her space career, we gradually discover that Cassie, focused and confident on the surface, harbours doubts of her own too.
Everything seems too neat, too schematic. Fehinti Balogun makes the most of Bryan, an underwritten figure who, for all his firmly held beliefs, is one of life’s avuncular peacemakers. Arterton, as Stella, is solid enough, but lacks emotional range. As the two women stake out their positions, it is Lydia Wilson’s Cassie who consistently holds your attention. Wilson’s eyes are always burning, yet she slowly lets us glimpse her inner fragility. It’s a wonderfully intense performance.
To June 12, atgtickets.com

https://www.thetimes.com/article/what-ex.title: What exactly does Black Lives Matter want?
https://www.thetimes.com/article/what-ex.text:
One year ago this week, a 46-year-old black man called George Floyd was murdered in Minneapolis by policeman Derek Chauvin. What followed was a surge of racial protest and activism that convulsed not just America but much of the world. From Paris to Cape Town to Tokyo, the words rang out: “Black Lives Matter”.
Across Britain, thousands marched, donated money and demanded change. The Black Lives Matter slogan became ubiquitous, appearing on the shirts of Premier League footballers, who continue to kneel before each game in solidarity. There were unprecedented conversations on race, slavery and the legacy of empire.
Black Lives Matter UK, the activist group founded as an offshoot of the American Black Lives Matter movement, was catapulted into the limelight. Its GoFundMe page raised £1.2 million from more than 35,000 donors. Its previously little-known organisers were suddenly featured in the national news. Smaller Black Lives Matter groups sprang up in towns and cities across the country.
A year on from Floyd’s death, many of these groups are planning to mark Tuesday’s anniversary with protests and vigils. But while the slogan continues to dominate the conversation around race in Britain, there is still uncertainty over what the British Black Lives Matter organisation is. How does it work? How does it spend its money? What does it want?
The answer, which varies slightly depending on who you ask, is true racial equality, the abolition of the police, the closure of prisons and revolutionary change to British society.
In the UK, the organisation is highly decentralised, with as many as 100 local groups, from BLM Cardiff & Vale and BLM Nottingham to BLM in the Stix, a network for rural supporters. Although the different groups often co-ordinate via WhatsApp, there is no central planning or committee, and they have sometimes found themselves at odds over policies and tactics.
The national group, Black Lives Matter UK, is the most prominent. Its platform calls for, among other things, an end to the sale and manufacture of arms in Britain; an end to police surveillance and armed police; an end to immigration enforcement in Britain; the abolition of tuition fees; and “an immediate reversal of all cuts made during austerity”. The platform carries the prominent American slogan “defund the police”.
“Our politics are the politics of abolition,” says Adam Elliott-Cooper, a longtime organiser with Black Lives Matter UK and research fellow in sociology at Greenwich University. “This doesn’t mean we’re going to close every prison tomorrow and sack every police officer the next day. What it does mean is that we want to make abolitionist reforms, which work towards this vision of a world in which police and prisons are obsolete.”
Instead of pouring money into Britain’s “bloated and failing prison and police border system”, Elliott-Cooper argues that investing in education, mental health and employment opportunities for poorer communities would reduce the need to have police in the first place.
Not all British BLM groups entirely agree on this point, according to Bianca Ali, 29, a comedian and charity fundraiser who is a founding member of BLM Cardiff & Vale. She points out that BLM Liverpool has advocated “reforming” rather than abolishing the police, whereas BLM Cardiff & Vale supports “defunding leading to abolition”.
Ali doesn’t believe the police can be reformed. “Abolition needs to happen, I hope to high God it does,” she says. “Every crime stems from mental health. If you take away the police, the crime rates will drop. Take the money and put it into mental health services for black and brown people, run by black and brown people, so that we can be understood by our own kind.”
As with most BLM activists, Ali doesn’t focus her attention on gang murders or violence between black men, viewing that discussion as an attempt to blame violence on individuals rather than the unfair system within which they operate.
“The violence is a reflection of a broken system,” she says. “The way that gangs emerge is through the breakdown of the systems, the breakdown of service. If we didn’t have so much institutionalised racism, then these types of things wouldn’t exist. Gang members don’t wake up as a child and say, ‘I’m going to be a gang member.’ They have bigger dreams, but these bigger dreams are not attainable for them.”
BLM UK recently announced where the first tranche of its donations, nearly £170,000, will be spent. In order for GoFundMe to release the money, the group had to hire lawyers and accountants. It has also registered as a “community benefit society” called Black Liberation Movement UK.
The beneficiaries include £7,500 to AZ Mag, an arts and culture initiative for LGBTQ+ people of colour, £7,500 to Sindicato de Manteros de Madrid, a Spanish labour union for street vendors, and £5,000 to A Tribe Named Athari, a pan-African, anti-colonial, youth-led organisation calling for transformative justice.
There was also £5,000 for All Black Lives UK, a youth-focused activist group that helped co-ordinate last summer’s George Floyd protests. They also helped organise the Bristol protest which pulled down the statue of the slave trader Edward Colston.
Tasha Johnson, 22, a co-founder of All Black Lives UK, hopes that young black people will be able to “live in the country they were born in without experiencing discrimination”. She believes pulling down statues is an important symbolic statement. “The statues are important to take down so we don’t glorify these people,” she says. “This country can’t seem to accept that it had a bad historical past. We’re supposed to be grateful that we’re able to learn about the history of my family being raped, we’re supposed to be grateful to live here.”
Black Lives Matter UK was founded in 2016 after a visit from a group of US activists including Patrisse Cullors, a leader of Black Lives Matter in America. But it was the surge of activism around George Floyd’s death that brought them to national prominence.
Cullors has attracted fervent debate in America for describing herself as a “trained Marxist”. Many BLM UK members echo her sentiments. “Not everyone in BLM is a Marxist, but I would say everyone is very critical of capitalism,” says Elliott-Cooper.
The various British Black Lives Matter groups intersect with a number of other causes and organisations on the left and far left. Many back the “Kill the Bill” coalition against the government’s Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Bill.
Some BLM UK members were previously involved with London Black Revolutionaries. Kwabena Devonish, 22, is a member of the Socialist Workers Party as well as being an organiser with BLM Cardiff & Vale. She views BLM as a “revolutionary” movement. “When people see BLM they think about George Floyd,” she says. “But it’s so much bigger than that. We have to change the system.”
On its Facebook page, BLM UK says it opposes a range of different prejudices, from “transphobia”, “racism” and “sexism” to “misogynoir” (discrimination against black women), “respectability politics”, “stereotypes” and “fatphobia”.
“I don’t think you can care about one social cause and not the rest of them,” says Johnson. “They all spout from the same place, it’s always injustice. Once you’re a part of one movement, you’re a part of all of them.”
Black liberation movements have a longstanding affinity for the Palestinian cause, and BLM has thrown itself into the fray. At a recent pro-Palestine protest outside Downing Street, Joshua Virasami, a leading BLM UK activist, explained this point. “In the Palestinian liberation lies the freedom of black people,” he told the crowd. “The ashram of liberation is a global one.”
At last week’s pro-Palestine rally outside the Israeli embassy in London, Virasami spoke again, quoting the writer James Baldwin: “Israel was not created for the salvation of the Jews,” he said. “Israel was created for the salvation of western interests.”
Virasami believes in violent action, and has twice found himself in court after demonstrations, once for storming a town hall in protest against gentrification. “We must situate the riot as a legitimate and necessarily violent form of protest in the struggle for freedom within racial capitalism,” he wrote in a recent article.
In terms of size and fundraising, BLM UK still pales in comparison to its older cousin in the US. Conversation across the Atlantic is common, though, as is the conviction that the roots of British and American racism are intertwined.
“Britain likes to imagine it has a different history to the US,” says Elliott-Cooper. “It forgets that it was the largest slaveholding nation in history, so it’s no surprise we have similar issues here in the UK.”
Devonish says she recently attended a meeting with the Communist Party of Detroit along with a US BLM chapter. “We do look for inspiration at the way they come together with other groups,” she says. “But I feel like sometimes people look to America too much. They try to use that to deflect what happens in Britain. The UK is the heart of colonialism, but people are always pointing the finger at America.”
American objectives often cross over to British BLM groups. Ibram X Kendi, a prominent US intellectual, popularised the idea of viewing the world through the prism of “racist” and “anti-racist”, arguing that in a racist society, there is no such thing as being neutral, one has to be actively anti-racist.
BLM in the Stix is organising around this idea. Gurpreet Kaur, 42, a charity consultant in Essex, joined BLM in the aftermath of Floyd’s death. “I felt like I was complicit in some way, because I wasn’t doing more,” she says. “I wasn’t racist, but I wasn’t anti-racist.”
She helps run BLM in the Stix, seeking to unite often isolated activists in different rural areas. “We want everyone who is not racist to become anti-racist,” she says. “We’re focused on people who sit at home, don’t say anything racist or do anything racist, but don’t do anything to actually help. We need white people to take on the fight.”
Kaur hopes to develop a kite mark or flag that town councils can use to highlight their town’s anti-racist stance. She believes it will help “people go to rural places and see that they’re friendly and anti-racist”.
Although the loose and at times barely connected coalition of British BLM groups has achieved much in the past year, some activists feel it would be better if there was a more formal and centralised movement directing their actions.
“We could benefit from some central organising,” says Ali. “We could definitely make more of an impact. But the truth is you don’t necessarily gel with everyone. You have to be on the same page personally as well as morally.”
Over time there has been pushback against BLM, most recently in the smattering of boos heard when players took the knee before Chelsea and Leicester City’s FA Cup final last weekend. Trevor Phillips, the former chairman of the Commission for Racial Equality, recently criticised BLM too.
“A lot of Black Lives Matter propaganda does not recognise that Britain is a very different place to the United States,” he said in an interview. “We should think of Black Lives Matter as much more like Extinction Rebellion [the radical environmentalist group]. They’re being used as a front for people who want to overthrow things as they are.”
Johnson sees this kind of backlash as evidence of how long a road BLM has before it. “The fact that there was such a racist response to the BLM protests shows we still have a long way to go.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.title: With a little help from its friends, Extinction Rebellion runs rings round the law
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.text:
As he sat in the dock last month awaiting the jury’s verdict, Ian Bray, 53, a co-founder of Extinction Rebellion, was prepared for the worst.
The salvage worker from Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, and five other climate change activists had admitted involvement in causing £25,000 damage to Shell’s London headquarters during a protest in 2019 — but had tried to argue that a “bigger crime” was being committed against the environment by the oil giant.
“They don’t have any defence in law for the charges they face,” Judge Gregory Perrins warned the jury at Southwark crown court in south London.
Bray recalled: “I was kind of expecting to sit there and be stitched up.” Instead, the jury of seven women and five men chose to defy the judge’s directions and cleared the six defendants of all charges. “People were in tears in the courtroom,” Bray said.
The unusual outcome preceded a string of court cases involving Extinction Rebellion (XR) members, who are being acquitted on technicalities or handed fines that amount to little more than a slap on the wrist.
“They seem to be running rings around the courts,” said one prosecuting barrister, who asked not to be named. “It’s a shrewd strategy.”
Last September XR blockaded newspaper printing plants at Broxbourne, Hertfordshire, and Knowsley, Merseyside. The plants are owned by News UK, publisher of The Sunday Times, The Times and The Sun, and also print copies of the Financial Times, the Daily Mail and The Daily Telegraph. Boris Johnson described the protests as “completely unacceptable”. Emily Thornberry, the shadow international trade secretary, said they were “very worrying” and “wrong”. At Broxbourne 3.5 million papers were prevented from hitting the newsstands. News UK said it lost £1 million as a result.
About 50 XR activists who took part in the Broxbourne blockade are due before St Albans magistrates’ court over the coming weeks. Last Monday the first six were found guilty of wilfully obstructing the highway but were given conditional discharges or fined as little as £150. The district judge, Sally Fudge, declared that no damage had been caused and rejected a request by prosecutors for the defendants to pay £5,000 compensation to News UK.
The trial had been delayed after one of the defendants, Liam Norton, 36, of Scarborough, glued his hand to the dock and started broadcasting proceedings on his phone. Wearing a pink superhero-style mask, Norton shouted at the judge: “Unfortunately, today the only response is to disobey in the dock and show contempt as you show contempt to this planet.” Norton was barred from attending the rest of the trial and arrested on suspicion of criminal damage before being released under investigation. His antics have been uploaded to XR’s YouTube channel.
XR makes no secret of its courtroom tactics, which it has branded as “Disobey in the dock”. A how-to video is available on the group’s main website. It features Cathy Eastburn, 53, a Cambridge graduate and musician, who was jailed for two weeks for contempt of court after gluing herself to a screen and livestreaming her plea hearing at Westminster magistrates’ court last November.
“I’m planning to disrupt proceedings,” she says in the clip on the eve of the hearing. “I’m not going to co-operate with the legal process tomorrow.”
Last week Rowan Tilly, 63, who halted traffic during a protest in Regent Street in October 2019, was said by XR to have been praised for her “sincerity” and her “noble” deeds by a district judge, Michael Bisgrove, at City of London magistrates’ court. Tilly, from Oxford, was given a rare absolute discharge (where a crime has technically been committed but no punishment is imposed) and ordered to pay £200 costs. According to an XR observer who attended the hearing, Bisgrove cited the suffragettes and US civil rights movement as facilitators of change when finding Tilly guilty of obstructing the highway.
Lord Hain, the former Labour cabinet minister and anti-apartheid campaigner, believes the Shell verdict last month should be viewed as a “test case”, indicating that XR has a significant amount of public sentiment on it side.
“The courts should be pursuing real criminals — terrorists, drug traffickers and the rest. Not climate change protesters,” he said.
Nazir Afzal, a former chief prosecutor for the northwest of England, said: “The judge is the arbiter of the law, but the jury is the arbiter of the facts. If they have gone against the instructions given to them by a judge, then there may be good reason for them doing so, and that might be them sending out a message about what they think about the law.” That is not much help to businesses that have been criminally damaged or people whose jobs and lives have been disrupted.
The writer Toby Young, general secretary of the Free Speech Union, said: “This effectively sends a message to other protest groups that if you want to try and shut down the free press, go ahead because you are only going to get a slap on the wrist. You undermine the rule of law if the police and courts don’t enforce the law without fear or favour.”
